# Seed-Level Demeaning LOGO

## Experiment

**Goal**: Address the seed-sharing confound. For each (seed, generator), subtract depth-0 feature values as a baseline, then classify gen-1 vs gen-2+ using only the delta features.

**Method**: For every (model_name, seed_id) group, compute Δfeature = feature(depth_k) - feature(depth_0). Drop depth-0 rows (Δ=0, would leak). Run standard 8-gen LOGO binary eval with XGBoost (same hyperparams as eval_8gen_logo.py).

**Data**: 37058 total rows -> 29095 after removing depth-0.

## Results

| Generator | Binary F1 | 95% CI |
|-----------|-----------|--------|
| pythia-1b | 0.7814 | [0.7664, 0.7967] |
| qwen3-1.7b | 0.7498 | [0.7342, 0.7630] |
| qwen3-0.6b | 0.7457 | [0.7295, 0.7608] |
| pythia-2.8b | 0.7352 | [0.7217, 0.7503] |
| olmo-2-1b | 0.6956 | [0.6792, 0.7105] |
| llama-3.2-3b | 0.6893 | [0.6748, 0.7037] |
| qwen3-8b | 0.6623 | [0.6461, 0.6786] |
| mistral-7b-v0.3 | 0.5472 | [0.5319, 0.5628] |
| **AVERAGE** | **0.7008** | |

## Interpretation

Average F1 = 0.7008, compared to the undemeaned baseline of 0.694.

The result falls within the expected range [0.674, 0.714], confirming: **depth signal is preserved after removing seed-level topic variation**. The classifier's ability to distinguish gen-1 from gen-2+ does not depend on seed-specific content; it relies on generative degradation patterns that persist across seeds.

Slight improvement (+0.7pp) suggests seed-level topic variation may have been mild noise rather than a helpful signal.

mistral-7b-v0.3 remains the weakest performer (0.547), consistent with prior LOGO results.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The near-stationarity of shape features is consistent with the softmax architecture and fixed sampling parameters constraining distributional shape while allowing location to drift.
Sampling ablation supports this as a tendency rather than a guarantee ($t \in [0.5, 0.7]$: ${\leq}0.3$\,pp degradation; $t = 1.0$: $-6$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), and prompt-type dependence further modulates the effect (elaboration F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ continuation 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).

Instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker fingerprints in preliminary experiments (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.763 base, 6-generator LOGO): alignment-imposed length regulation and format constraints compress the distributional variation that DDR exploits.
This restricts current applicability to base models and constitutes the primary scope limitation.
At the document level within base models, gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for automated filtering but sufficient for corpus-level flagging; the gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ boundary concentrates 86\% of binary errors as false negatives, with larger generators exacerbating this (Mistral-7B error rate 45\% vs.\ Pythia-1B 18\%; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Cross-temperature transfer degrades substantially ($t{=}0.7 \to t{=}1.0$: Qwen3-1.7B F1 drops from 0.789 to 0.418; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}).
A scale-dependent degradation trend is visible: binary F1 decreases from 0.718--0.724 (1--2.8B parameters) to 0.692 (8B) and 0.633 (7B), consistent with larger models compressing the feature margins DDR exploits.

Three classes represent the practical resolution ceiling: 5-class F1 drops to ${\approx}$0.50 (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}), and ordinal-specific methods (CORAL, Frank-Hall) yield no improvement over standard XGBoost (Appendix~\ref{app:classifier}). These results suggest that the gen-1/gen-2+ boundary rather than ordinal structure is the bottleneck.
DDR is distinct from model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}: inference-chain drift occurs with fixed parameters, is fully reversible, and leaves distributional shape comparatively stable. This pattern suggests compression within existing capacity rather than erosion of it.
Levene tests reject strict equal-variance for all features ($p < 10^{-10}$), but shape-feature variance ratios (0.98--1.12) are an order of magnitude closer to unity than drifting-feature ratios (1.90--2.20), supporting the characterization as comparatively stable rather than strictly invariant.

2	\label{sec:limitations}
3	
4	All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
5	This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects and enable controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
6	However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
7	Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 base); these comparisons use earlier LOGO subsets (5--6 generators) predating the full 8-generator expansion in Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}.
8	Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
9	Extending depth fingerprinting to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.
10	
11	Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
12	Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
13	Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.
14

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects and enable controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 base); these comparisons use earlier LOGO subsets (5--6 generators) predating the full 8-generator expansion in Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}.
Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
Extending depth fingerprinting to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

Differential depth response strength is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains show strongest drift (within-type F1\,=\,0.781) compared to elaboration (0.730), rewriting (0.737), and paraphrastic chains (binary F1\,=\,0.671 vs.\ 0.749 for continuation).
DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.809, binary F1\,=\,0.764), though the eight generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.
Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).
All seed texts in the main evaluation are English Wikipedia excerpts.
Cross-domain evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}) shows that depth signal persists across News, Academic, and Code domains (binary F1 $>$ 0.73 under LOGO at $t{=}1.0$), though a domain $\times$ temperature interaction exists: certain domain/generator combinations at lower temperature approach chance level (e.g., Academic domain binary F1\,=\,0.628 at $t{=}0.7$), which suggests that reference model calibration is critical for cross-domain deployment.
The reference model dependency (Pythia-410M, English-centric pretraining) limits non-English applicability and adds inference overhead relative to surface-feature-only approaches.
Generalization to other languages remains untested.

Our default analysis uses fixed decoding parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p{=}0.9$). A sampling ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}) shows robustness to moderate variation ($t \in [0.5, 0.7]$, ${\leq}0.3$\,pp) but substantial degradation at $t{=}1.0$ ($-6$\,pp), which indicates that depth fingerprinting assumes standard decoding regimes.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+). A 5-class evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}) yields LOGO F1\,$\approx$\,0.50, with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable, validating the 3-class design as the practical resolution limit.

% Abstract — Depth Fingerprinting of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
LLM-generated text increasingly re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation, and the resulting recursive chains progressively diverge from human-written text.
We ask whether this drift is structured enough to classify how many generation steps a text has undergone, framing this as \emph{generation depth classification} (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ rather than binary real-vs-synthetic).
Studying eight base (pretrained) models from five families (0.6B--8B parameters), we identify a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): central-tendency features (mean entropy, lexical diversity) drift monotonically with generation depth, while shape features (entropy max, vocabulary tail slope) remain near-stationary, consistent with a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution whose shape remains comparatively stable.
A 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 under eight-generator leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) evaluation and 0.764 on cross-model chains (five-generator subset), using a single 410M-parameter reference model.
The depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning, which restricts current applicability to base models.
\end{abstract}

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	When LLM outputs are fed back as inputs to subsequent generation, the resulting recursive chains form a dynamical system whose distributional properties evolve with each step.
5	How this evolution proceeds is a fundamental question that connects to both model collapse theory \cite{curse_of_recursion, self_consuming_mad} and data provenance.
6	Estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}, evidence that LLM text already re-enters training pipelines at scale.
7	Yet existing detection methods \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide only binary real-vs-synthetic decisions and obscure qualitative differences: a first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.
8	
9	We formulate \emph{generation depth classification}, classifying text by generation depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than a binary label, and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
10	No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When LLM outputs are fed back as inputs to subsequent generation, the resulting recursive chains form a dynamical system whose distributional properties evolve with each step.
How this evolution proceeds is a fundamental question that connects to both model collapse theory \cite{curse_of_recursion, self_consuming_mad} and data provenance.
Estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}, evidence that LLM text already re-enters training pipelines at scale.
Yet existing detection methods \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide only binary real-vs-synthetic decisions and obscure qualitative differences: a first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.

We formulate \emph{generation depth classification}, classifying text by generation depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than a binary label, and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.

The key finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): when we measure how eight base-model generators from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B--8B parameters) transform text across recursive depths, central-tendency and diversity features (reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) drift monotonically, while shape features (entropy max, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution with distributional shape remaining comparatively stable: the softmax architecture and fixed sampling parameters constrain distributional shape under standard decoding regimes, while each successive generation compresses the location toward the model's preferred output distribution.
While distributional drift under recursive generation is documented in the model collapse literature \cite{curse_of_recursion, self_consuming_mad}, the structured decomposition into monotonically drifting and near-stationary components, and its exploitation for depth classification, has not been previously reported.
We restrict to base (pretrained) models as a deliberate design choice, since instruction-tuning introduces confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven shaping) that obscure this intrinsic mechanism; preliminary experiments confirm substantially degraded depth signal under instruction tuning (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that, under eight-generator leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) evaluation, achieves leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 and 0.764 on cross-model chains (five-generator subset), using a single 410M-parameter reference model.
Multi-detector ensembles achieve moderately higher F1 at 2.4$\times$ the computational cost (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).
The signal is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains show stronger drift than elaboration or rewriting (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

Our empirical contributions are twofold:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item We formulate generation depth classification, moving beyond binary real-vs-synthetic detection to classify text as gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+, and construct an evaluation suite of 37K texts from eight base-model generators spanning five families (0.6B--8B parameters).
    \item We characterize a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): central-tendency features drift monotonically with generation depth ($|\rho| > 0.60$) while shape features remain comparatively stable ($|\rho| < 0.10$). This decomposition is novel relative to aggregate drift observations in the model collapse literature.
\end{enumerate}
